analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addressed the need for advanced planning and adaptable response strategies to prevent measles transmission in healthcare facilities, motivated by the re-emergence of measles and the risk of outbreaks in high-exposure settings such as the Veterans Affairs (VA) system.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A measles management plan was developed and implemented by an Infection Prevention and Control (IPAC) team in response to a cluster of measles cases within the VA healthcare system, with modifications made as the cluster unfolded.
analysis.methods: The IPAC team initiated a multi-disciplinary approach and created a measles preparedness plan encompassing guidance and education, early detection and testing, isolation and patient movement, and contact tracing and exposure management.
analysis.main_results: The first case resulted in 539 exposed patients, the second in 87 exposures, and the third in no exposures; despite extensive exposure, zero secondary measles cases were reported.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Proactive planning enabled rapid response to the first case and controlled secondary transmission, while delayed identification of the first case caused significant exposures, highlighting the importance of timely detection and iterative plan refinement.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings may guide other healthcare facilities in improving measles preparedness and response, emphasizing the value of structured frameworks and real-time adaptations to mitigate transmission risks.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is limited by the absence of detailed demographic or clinical characteristics of exposed individuals and the lack of statistical analysis to quantify the impact of specific interventions, warranting cautious interpretation of the zero secondary cases.

analysis.summary_en: This study describes the development and iterative refinement of a measles preparedness plan by a Veterans Affairs (VA) Infection Prevention and Control team in response to a cluster of measles cases. The plan included guidance and education, early detection and testing, isolation and patient movement, and contact tracing and exposure management. Despite extensive exposure from the first two cases (539 and 87 exposed patients, respectively), no secondary measles cases occurred, attributed to proactive planning and rapid response. However, delayed recognition of the initial case led to significant exposures, underscoring the critical role of timely detection. The findings suggest that structured, adaptable frameworks can effectively mitigate measles transmission in healthcare settings, offering practical guidance for other facilities.

papers.title: Immune responses elicited by rMV-SLAMblind oncolytic therapy exert a synergistic effect on cancer therapy
papers.abstract: Abstract Oncolytic virotherapy has emerged as a promising strategy for cancer therapy. rMV-SLAMblind is a recombinant measles virus that lacks the ability to interact with SLAM and specifically infects and lyses NECTIN4 + cancer cells. We previously reported that rMV-SLAMblind oncolytic virotherapy (rMV-OVT) exerts anti-tumor immunity through the activation of immune cells in virus-treated tumors. It is thought that oncolytic virotherapy promotes anti-tumor effects via two mechanisms: direct tumor cell lysis caused by infection and the induction of immune cell-mediated tumor cell death. However, it is unknown whether the immune cells activated by rMV-OVT exert anti-tumor effects on non-treated tumors and whether rMV-SLAMblind enhances the effects of immune checkpoint blockade. This study demonstrated that rMV-OVT suppressed the growth of non-treated tumors in a bilateral tumor mouse model and enhanced anti-tumor effects in combination therapy with anti-PD1 antibody. Notably, CD4 + T cell depletion led to the trends towards favorable anti-tumor effects of rMV-OVT in some cases, which was accompanied by increasing numbers of activated CD8 + T cells. These results suggest that rMV-OVT demonstrated efficacy via immune cell-mediated tumor cell death, which was improved by combination therapy with immune checkpoint inhibitors. These findings provide valuable insights into improving the efficacy of rMV-OVT for cancer therapy.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Oncolytic virotherapy has shown promise for cancer treatment, but it remains unknown whether immune responses elicited by rMV-SLAMblind oncolytic therapy can exert anti-tumor effects on non-treated tumors and whether this approach enhances the efficacy of immune checkpoint blockade.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study used a bilateral tumor mouse model to evaluate the anti-tumor effects of rMV-SLAMblind oncolytic virotherapy (rMV-OVT) and its combination with anti-PD1 antibody.
analysis.methods: The authors assessed tumor growth suppression in treated and non-treated tumors following rMV-OVT administration and evaluated the impact of CD4+ T cell depletion on anti-tumor responses.
analysis.main_results: rMV-OVT suppressed the growth of non-treated tumors in the bilateral tumor mouse model and enhanced anti-tumor effects when combined with anti-PD1 antibody.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that rMV-OVT exerts anti-tumor effects through immune cell-mediated tumor cell death, which is further improved by combination therapy with immune checkpoint inhibitors.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results provide insights into optimizing rMV-SLAMblind oncolytic virotherapy for cancer treatment, particularly in enhancing systemic anti-tumor immunity.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to a mouse model, and the evidence strength is moderate due to the absence of human data and potential confounding from immune cell depletion effects.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated whether rMV-SLAMblind oncolytic virotherapy (rMV-OVT) can induce anti-tumor immunity in non-treated tumors and enhance the effects of immune checkpoint blockade. Using a bilateral tumor mouse model, the authors demonstrated that rMV-OVT suppressed growth in non-treated tumors and improved anti-tumor responses when combined with anti-PD1 antibody. The findings suggest that rMV-OVT mediates tumor cell death via immune activation, which is further augmented by checkpoint inhibition. While promising, the study is limited to preclinical mouse data, and the evidence strength is moderate due to the lack of human validation and potential confounding from immune cell depletion.

elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果表明,rMV-OVT 通过免疫细胞介导的肿瘤细胞死亡发挥抗肿瘤作用,与免疫检查点抑制剂联合治疗可进一步改善这种作用。

papers.abstract_zh: 摘要 溶瘤病毒疗法已成为一种有前途的癌症治疗策略。rMV-SLAMblind 是一种重组 麻疹病毒,缺乏与 SLAM 相互作用的能力,并且特异性感染和裂解 NECTIN4 + 癌细胞。我们之前报道过rMV-SLAM盲溶瘤病毒疗法(rMV-OVT)通过激活病毒治疗的肿瘤中的免疫细胞来发挥抗肿瘤免疫力。据认为,溶瘤病毒疗法通过两种机制促进抗肿瘤作用:感染引起的直接肿瘤细胞裂解和诱导免疫细胞介导的肿瘤细胞死亡。然而,rMV-OVT激活的免疫细胞是否对未治疗的肿瘤发挥抗肿瘤作用以及rMV-SLAMblind是否增强免疫检查点阻断的效果尚不清楚。这项研究表明,rMV-OVT 可抑制双侧肿瘤小鼠模型中未治疗肿瘤的生长,并增强与抗 PD1 抗体联合治疗的抗肿瘤效果。值得注意的是,在某些情况下,CD4 + T 细胞耗竭导致 rMV-OVT 具有良好的抗肿瘤作用,同时伴随着激活的 CD8 + T 细胞数量的增加。这些结果表明,rMV-OVT 通过免疫细胞介导的肿瘤细胞死亡发挥功效,并通过与免疫检查点抑制剂的联合治疗得到改善。这些发现为提高 rMV-OVT 癌症治疗功效提供了宝贵的见解。

time: 1 min (375 words) Event highlights On 17–18 August, in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, WHO, in collaboration with the Ministry of Health of Kyrgyzstan and with the support of the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, conducted an assessment of the country’s response to the recent measles outbreak. Kyrgyzstan remains among the 10 countries in the WHO European Region with the highest number of reported measles cases, following an outbreak that began in early 2023 and rapidly spread across all regions of the country. In response, the Kyrgyz government, with WHO’s technical support, organized several large-scale supplementary immunization activities. The first 2 rounds, conducted in 2023 and 2024, targeted children aged 9–84 months in 7 regions, achieving vaccination coverage of 85% and 79%, respectively. A third round in 2024, funded by the government and covering Jalal-Abad region, achieved 88% coverage. A fourth round, supported by Gavi and launched in October 2024, is still ongoing, with vaccination coverage reaching 74% by 11 December 2024. Against this backdrop, the assessment aimed to analyse the actions taken by the national health system to respond to the measles outbreak. It identified immediate and longer-term corrective actions to strengthen preparedness and response; developed an action plan to address key gaps and challenges, and make recommendations for strengthening the measles response; and integrated measles preparedness into wider health security planning. The assessment focused on the following key areas and functions: national planning, response coordination and epidemiological surveillance, including the identification, investigation and monitoring of measles cases; risk communication, including community engagement and communication with the public; and vaccination, including vaccine procurement, supply and delivery. Around 40 representatives of national public health organizations from Bishkek and various regions of the country, as well as international health partners, participated in the assessment. Through document reviews, presentations and facilitated group discussions, participants assessed the actions taken during the outbreak, identified strengths and gaps, and drew lessons to inform future preparedness and response. The assessment culminated in a set of priority recommendations and a practical action plan aimed at addressing identified gaps and strengthening Kyrgyzstan’s capacity to prevent, detect and respond effectively to measles outbreaks and other vaccine-preventable disease threats. This event was co-funded by the European Union through the EU4Health programme, and was also supported by Gavi

Weekend Disease Reporting Hotline: 1-800-362-2736 Skip to Main Content Measles Outbreak in Iowa On August 17, 2026, the Iowa Department of Health and Human Services (Iowa HHS) confirmed 12 measles cases in Iowa with evidence of person-to-person spread. Iowa HHS and local health officials have identified locations visited by individuals while contagious, where others might have been exposed to measles. Anyone present at these locations during the listed date and time should monitor for symptoms of measles. If you think you have been exposed to measles and have symptoms, call your medical provider or nearest emergency room BEFORE you arrive to avoid exposing other people. The best way to prevent measles is to get vaccinated. The MMR vaccine is safe, thoroughly tested, and incredibly effective in protecting both you and your community. Two doses, given at least 28 days apart, offer the best protection. Visit our Measles page for vaccination recommendations based on your age and risk level. The outbreak is linked to specific locations visited by individuals while contagious, potentially exposing others. If exposed and symptomatic, individuals are advised to contact their medical providers before arriving to avoid spreading the virus further. The response includes monitoring for symptoms and promoting vaccination as the best prevention method. The outbreak is currently under investigation, and the public is encouraged to follow health guidelines to protect their community.

news.content_zh: 弗吉尼亚州卫生部 (VDH) 于 2026 年 8 月 19 日发布了更新,重点介绍了弗吉尼亚州免疫宣传月期间的 麻疹 疫苗 建议和免疫工作。该报告强调了常规免疫接种对于保护儿童和社区免受 麻疹 和其他 疫苗 可预防疾病的重要性。虽然没有报告确认的 麻疹 暴发 或具体病例编号,但 VDH 正在与利益相关者合作,确保家庭能够使用 疫苗接种。该文件没有提供有关 暴发 规模、风险级别或具体公共卫生应对措施的详细信息。重点是提高免疫接种的认识和可及性,而不是详细说明有效的 暴发 或其影响。VDH 还提到了其他公共卫生举措,例如紫外线防护和孕产妇健康,但这些与 麻疹 没有直接关系。该报告不包括任何与麻疹相关的确诊或疑似病例、死亡或暴露情况,也没有概述具体的遏制或调查措施。

(FOX 6) - The Wisconsin Department of Health Services confirmed 15 cases of measles Thursday, with an additional 6 probable cases. This was a jump from 2 confirmed cases last Tuesday. Measles outbreak in Lafayette and Iowa Counties What we know: According to Dr. Ryan Westergaard with the Wisconsin DHS, the department is working closely with local health officials in Lafayette and Iowa counties, as well as getting national support from the Centers of Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) to investigate the cases, trace exposure and contain further spread. What we don't know: At this time, the Wisconsin DHS states it has not identified any public exposure locations and is currently confidentially contacting those who have developed measles to trace the source of the disease. The rapid emergence of cases among those who have not traveled outside Wisconsin suggests there is active local transmission, Westergaard explained. This makes additional cases within the community that have not yet been identified or reported to public health services likely. Preventing measles What you can do: The best thing to do to prevent measles transmission is to receive the MMR vaccine. Two doses of the measles vaccine are 97% effective at preventing the disease, while one dose is 93% effective at preventing measles, according to the CDC. You can check your vaccine status using the Wisconsin Immunization Registry, which is an online database that tracks vaccine records for Wisconsinites. You can also contact your healthcare provider. Guidance on whether you should receive a measles vaccine booster is also provided by the Wisconsin DHS. If you were born before 1957, you do not need a measles booster because you were likely already exposed to the disease. If you were vaccinated between 1957-1989 you may benefit from a measles booster. Some vaccines used between 1963 and 1967 were inactive. You should contact your healthcare provider for more guidance. If you were vaccinated after 1989, you have likely received two doses of the measles vaccine and have effective protection against the disease. DHS is also asking people to be familiar with the symptoms of measles. If you do go to a healthcare provider, it is important that you call them in advance to inform them of your potential measles status, so that they can take precautions to prevent further spread of the disease. Measles symptoms Dig deeper: Measles is an extremely contagious disease. If one person has measles, up to 90% of people who come into close contact with that person will become infected if they are not protected, according to the CDC. The disease spreads when an infected person coughs or sneezes, making it an airborne virus. A person can contract measles simply by being in a room where an infected person with measles has been up to two hours after the person has already left the room. You can also get measles by touching an infected surface and then touching your eyes, nose or mouth. This means that the disease can be contracted anywhere in public life. Measles symptoms: Symptoms of measles typically begin to develop 10 to 21 days after infection. Symptoms include: Runny nose High fever (could be above 104 degrees Fahrenheit) Fatigue Cough Red, watery eyes, known as conjunctivitis, or "pink eye" A red rash with raised bumps that starts at the hairline and moves to the arms and legs three to five days after symptoms begin Rash that spreads all over the body, usually beginning three to five days after initial symptoms Measles complications: One out of every four people who get measles in the U.S. will be hospitalized, and up to two out of every 1,000 children who contract measles in the U.S. will die, even with advanced healthcare. These are other groups of people at higher risk of experiencing severe measles complications: Children younger than 5 years old Adults older than 20 years old Pregnant women Those with weakened immune systems, such as from leukemia or HIV Serious health complications that can come as a result of measles infection include pneumonia, brain damage caused by swelling, and deafness. While common complications include ear infections and diarrhea. Measles cases on the rise The backstory: Measles outbreaks have been on the rise in recent years. In 2025, the U.S. had more reported measles cases, outbreaks, affected states, and deaths than in any year since 1992, according to a study by KFF, a nonpartisan health policy research organization. Of the measles cases in the U.S. contracted between 2025-2026, over 90% of the cases were seen in unvaccinated people. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) National measles vaccination levels have also decreased over the past five years, with kindergarten and childhood measles coverage rates dipping to 92.5%, well below the 95% threshold needed to prevent transmission of measles virus. In Wisconsin, the CDC cites during the 2024-2025 school year, only about 85% of kindergartners in the state were vaccinated against measles, ranking lower than the national average. Map showing measles vaccination rates across the U.S. with data from the CDC. (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) Measles was declared eliminated from the United States in 2000, according to the CDC. This means there was no continuous spread of measles for longer than 12 months. The U.S. is on the verge of losing its measles elimination status, as Canada did in late 2025, according to The Associated Press. Routine childhood vaccination schedules executive order Big picture view: President Donald Trump announced an executive order last week aimed at childhood vaccinations that would require separating combination shots, including the measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine into separate injections. During the signing of his order, Trump repeated false claims about vaccinations, including their relationship to autism and that the MMR vaccine could be lethal, according to the AP. Trump's executive order calls for federal officials to develop plans within 90 days for breaking up the MMR shot and spacing out other vaccines. However, pharmaceutical scientists and former regulators contend that those revisions would take years and require drug manufacturers to spend millions of dollars on new studies and manufacturing facilities. Many public health experts were quick to condemn the president's executive order, according to the AP. Dr. Paul Offit, a Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia vaccine researcher and former government adviser, said the recommendations by Trump and Health and Human Services Sec. Robert F. Kennedy Jr."are just not science based," and it’s irresponsible to cast doubt on a vaccine that protects against measles when the nation is facing its biggest epidemic in more than 30 years, according to the AP. Right now, there are no individual vaccines in the U.S. for measles, mumps or rubella. Every vaccine approved for those viruses by the Food and Drug Administration is combination shots. Local perspective: The Wisconsin DHS Secretary put out a statement on Thursday regarding the president's executive order, continuing to back previous guidance from public health officials that supports the current recommended MMR vaccine. "There is no new scientific evidence that justifies changing recommendations that have, and continue to, protect children across the United States," wrote DHS Secretary Kirsten Johnson. In February, Wisconsin was among states that sued the Trump administration over previous changes to federal childhood vaccine recommendations. The Source: Information from this article was sourced from the Wisconsin Department of Health Services, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, KFF, and the Associated Press. This story was reported from Eden Prairie, Minnesota. analysis.time: Published 17 August 2026 at 12:25 CDT; event period spans from at least 12 August (2 confirmed cases) to 17 August 2026 (15 confirmed cases).
analysis.location_and_population: Wisconsin, USA; specifically Lafayette and Iowa counties; affected population includes unvaccinated individuals and those with incomplete vaccination status.
analysis.event: The Wisconsin Department of Health Services (DHS) confirmed 15 measles cases on 15 August 2026, up from 2 cases on 12 August 2026, indicating a rapidly expanding outbreak. The event is confirmed and under active investigation.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: 15 confirmed measles cases and 6 probable cases as of 15 August 2026. Risk of additional undetected cases is high due to active local transmission and high contagiousness (up to 90% secondary attack rate among unprotected contacts). Measles is an airborne virus with potential for severe complications, including hospitalization (1 in 4 cases) and death (up to 2 per 1,000 children).
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Wisconsin DHS, local health officials, and CDC are investigating, tracing exposures, and containing spread. No public exposure locations identified; source of infection remains under confidential investigation. DHS advises vaccination (MMR), checking immunization records via the Wisconsin Immunization Registry, and contacting healthcare providers for guidance on boosters. Current status is under investigation with unresolved source identification.

analysis.brief_en: Wisconsin health authorities reported 15 confirmed measles cases on 15 August 2026, a sharp rise from just two cases three days earlier, signaling active local transmission in Lafayette and Iowa counties. The Wisconsin Department of Health Services, working with local and CDC teams, is tracing exposures and attempting to identify the infection source while warning that additional undetected cases are likely. Measles, an airborne virus with a 90% secondary infection rate among unvaccinated contacts, poses high risks of severe outcomes, including hospitalization and death. Public health officials urge immediate vaccination with two doses of the MMR vaccine, which is 97% effective, and advise checking immunization records via the state registry. The outbreak underscores broader national concerns, as U.S. measles vaccination coverage has fallen below the 95% threshold needed to prevent transmission, threatening the country’s 2000 elimination status.

news.content_title: State health officials confirm 12 new measles cases in Iowa
news.content: News Sports Opinion Business Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals IOWA State health officials confirm 12 new measles cases in Iowa Norah Judson Des Moines Register Aug. 17, 2026Updated Aug. 18, 2026, 7:09 p.m. CT (This story was updated because it contained an inaccuracy.) The Iowa Department of Health and Human Services has confirmed 12 new cases of measles in the state, bringing the total for 2026 to 13. Last year, the state reported just nine cases. According to a Monday, Aug. 17, news release, the outbreak is in southern Iowa. DHHS believes person-to-person transmission has played a role in the spread of the highly contagious illness and said it is working with local public health agencies to ensure affected families and communities have access to care and vaccination. Places and times infected individuals could have spread measles DHHS says the infected individuals visited: Natural Grocers, 8650 Hickman Road, Clive, between 2:30 and 5 p.m. July 28. Vero Health Center, 630 S 50th St., West Des Moines, between 3:30 and 6:30 p.m. July 28. Office Depot, 3910 University Ave., West Des Moines, between 5 and 7:30 p.m. July 28. Menards, 12000 Hickman Road, Clive, between 6 and 8:30 p.m. July 28. Menards, 6000 SE 14th St., Des Moines, between 7 and 9:30 p.m. July 28. Wells Hometown Drug, 208 E Franklin St., Bloomfield, between 4:30 and 7 p.m. July 30. JR Feed and Supply, 17599 200th St., Bloomfield, between 8:30 a.m. and 6 p.m. Aug. 9. What is measles and what are the symptoms? Measles is a viral illness with symptoms that include fever, cough, red and watery eyes, a runny nose and a rash. Symptoms may appear from seven to 14 days after contact with someone who is infected and contagious. The virus is spread through the air when an infected person coughs, sneezes and breathes and can remain virulent for up to two hours. According to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 90% of people who come into contact with the virus become infected if they are unvaccinated, making it one of the most contagious diseases known. Additionally, 1 in 5 of those people end up hospitalized, according to the CDC. Measles can cause health complications including ear infections and diarrhea, as well as pneumonia, swelling of the brain and in some cases, death. Children are most at risk for serious complications. In 2025, there was a total of nine measles cases in Iowa and 2,289 across the country, with 243 patients hospitalized and three deaths, according to the DHHS. This year is set to outpace 2025, with 2,170 confirmed cases so far nationwide and more than four months remaining. All but 10% of infections occurred in people who were unvaccinated or had unknown vaccination status. How can I avoid getting measles? Measles is a vaccine-preventable disease. The MMR vaccine (measles, mumps and rubella) protects against measles with 97% efficacy, and is typically administered to children as part of the regular vaccine course, with the first dose when the child is 12 to 15 months of age and the second at 4 to 6 years. "The routine childhood immunization series is still our strongest protection against measles infection," Dr. Robert Kruse, director of the DHHS, said in the release. The recent increase in measles outbreaks has been attributed to plummeting vaccination rates. What to do if you believe you are infected with measles Those who may have been exposed to the infected individual are asked to monitor for symptoms for up to 21 days and to call their medical provider or the nearest emergency room before arrival and tell them they have been exposed to measles and have symptoms. CORRECTION: A previous version of this article had an incomplete number of measles cases in Iowa. The southern Iowa outbreak contains 12 cases, making 13 total cases in Iowa for 2026. USA Today staff writer Mary Walrath-Holridge and Des Moines Register staff writer Kyle Werner contributed to this article. Norah Judson is a staff writer for the Register. news.source_body_en: Iowa health officials confirmed 12 new measles cases in 2026, raising the state’s total to 13, with the outbreak concentrated in southern Iowa. The surge follows a national trend: 2,170 U.S. cases have been reported so far this year, already nearing 2025’s total of 2,289, which included 243 hospitalizations and three deaths. Public health authorities attribute the rise to plummeting vaccination rates, noting that 90% of infections occur in unvaccinated individuals. The Iowa Department of Health and Human Services is coordinating with local agencies to trace contacts, provide vaccinations, and warn exposed residents to monitor for symptoms for up to three weeks.

FOX 32 Minneapolis News - FOX 9 Detroit News - FOX 2 LiveNOW from FOX Contact Us Contests Sign up for email alerts FOX6 Mobile Apps FOX6 News Team Jobs at FOX6 EEO Report Public File Help FCC Applications Closed Captioning Info DTV Reception Questions Sales & Advertising FOX6 Sales Team Advertise with FOX6 FOX FOCUS Sponsored content Stream on FOX One Where to watch NFL Where to watch College Football Where to watch MLB Where to watch NASCAR Cup Series Where to watch IndyCar Where to watch Men's College Basketball Where to watch Women's College Basketball Where to watch WNBA Games Where to watch MLS Games Severe Thunderstorm Watch until FRI 10:00 PM CDT, Jefferson County, Walworth County, Kenosha County Wisconsin measles cases reach 36, more than doubling in past week By Maureen Breslin FOX6 News Milwaukee Health Published August 18, 2026 5:24 PM CDT Share Copy Link Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Reddit Published August 18, 2026 5:24 PM CDT article (Photo by Joe Raedle/Getty Images) ((Photo by Joe Raedle/Getty Images) / Getty Images) The Brief The Wisconsin Department of Health Services has confirmed that measles cases in the state have risen to 36 confirmed cases and three probable cases. These cases have been confirmed in Lafayette, Grant and Iowa counties and are all related. Those who are unvaccinated remain the most at risk for measles. MILWAUKEE - The Wisconsin Department of Health Services has now confirmed 36 measles cases as of Tuesday. This is a jump up from 15 cases that were confirmed last Thursday. More measles cases confirmed in Grant County What we know: In addition to the previous outbreaks in Lafayette and Iowa counties, two cases have been confirmed in Grant County, according to the Wisconsin DHS. There are also three additional probable cases in the area. These cases are all related to the prior cases within the southwestern Wisconsin region and bring the total known outbreak numbers to 36. According to Dr. Ryan Westergaard with the Wisconsin DHS, the department is working closely with local health officials in Lafayette and Iowa counties, as well as getting national support from the Centers of Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) to investigate the cases, trace exposure and contain further spread. What we don't know: At this time, the Wisconsin DHS states it has not identified any public exposure locations and is currently confidentially contacting those who have developed measles to trace the source of the disease. The rapid emergence of cases among those who have not traveled outside Wisconsin suggests there is active local transmission, Westergaard explained. This makes additional cases within the community that have not yet been identified or reported to public health services likely. Preventing measles What you can do: The best thing to do to prevent measles transmission is to receive the MMR vaccine. Two doses of the measles vaccine are 97% effective at preventing the disease, while one dose is 93% effective at preventing measles, according to the CDC. You can check your vaccine status using the Wisconsin Immunization Registry, which is an online database that tracks vaccine records for Wisconsinites. You can also contact your healthcare provider. Guidance on whether you should receive a measles vaccine booster is also provided by the Wisconsin DHS. If you were born before 1957, you do not need a measles booster because you were likely already exposed to the disease. If you were vaccinated between 1957-1989 you may benefit from a measles booster. Some vaccines used between 1963 and 1967 were inactive. You should contact your healthcare provider for more guidance. If you were vaccinated after 1989, you have likely received two doses of the measles vaccine and have effective protection against the disease. DHS is also asking people to be familiar with the symptoms of measles. If you do go to a healthcare provider, it is important that you call them in advance to inform them of your potential measles status, so that they can take precautions to prevent further spread of the disease. Measles symptoms Dig deeper: Measles is an extremely contagious disease. If one person has measles, up to 90% of people who come into close contact with that person will become infected if they are not protected, according to the CDC. The disease spreads when an infected person coughs or sneezes, making it an airborne virus. A person can contract measles simply by being in a room where an infected person with measles has been up to two hours after the person has already left the room. You can also get measles by touching an infected surface and then touching your eyes, nose or mouth. This means that the disease can be contracted anywhere in public life. Measles symptoms Symptoms of measles typically begin to develop 10 to 21 days after infection. Symptoms include: Runny nose High fever (could be above 104 degrees Fahrenheit) Fatigue Cough Red, watery eyes, known as conjunctivitis, or "pink eye" A red rash with raised bumps that starts at the hairline and moves to the arms and legs three to five days after symptoms begin Rash that spreads all over the body, usually beginning three to five days after initial symptoms Measles complications One out of every four people who get measles in the U.S. will be hospitalized, and up to two out of every 1,000 children who contract measles in the U.S. will die, even with advanced healthcare. These are other groups of people at higher risk of experiencing severe measles complications: Children younger than 5 years old Adults older than 20 years old Pregnant women Those with weakened immune systems, such as from leukemia or HIV Serious health complications that can come as a result of measles infection include pneumonia, brain damage caused by swelling, and deafness. While common complications include ear infections and diarrhea. Measles cases on the rise The backstory: Measles outbreaks have been on the rise in recent years. In 2025, the U.S. had more reported measles cases, outbreaks, affected states, and deaths than in any year since 1992, according to a study by KFF, a nonpartisan health policy research organization. Of the measles cases in the U.S. contracted between 2025-2026, over 90% of the cases were seen in unvaccinated people. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) National measles vaccination levels have also decreased over the past five years, with kindergarten and childhood measles coverage rates dipping to 92.5%, well below the 95% threshold needed to prevent transmission of measles virus. In Wisconsin, the CDC cites during the 2024-2025 school year, only about 85% of kindergartners in the state were vaccinated against measles, ranking lower than the national average. Exemptions are on the rise as well. For the 2025-2026 school year, 8.2% of Wisconsin parents got exemptions for their children to not receive vaccinations, and the vast majority of these exemptions were non-medical. Map showing measles vaccination rates across the U.S. with data from the CDC. (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) Measles was declared eliminated from the United States in 2000, according to the CDC. This means there was no continuous spread of measles for longer than 12 months. The U.S. is on the verge of losing its measles elimination status, as Canada did in late 2025, according to The Associated Press. Routine childhood vaccination schedules executive order Big picture view: President Donald Trump announced an executive order last week aimed at childhood vaccinations that would require separating combination shots, including the measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine into separate injections. During the signing of his order, Trump repeated false claims about vaccinations, including their relationship to autism and that the MMR vaccine could be lethal, according to the AP. Trump's executive order calls for federal officials to develop plans within 90 days for breaking up the MMR shot and spacing out other vaccines. However, pharmaceutical scientists and former regulators contend that those revisions would take years and require drug manufacturers to spend millions of dollars on new studies and manufacturing facilities. Many public health experts were quick to condemn the president's executive order, according to the AP. Dr. Paul Offit, a Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia vaccine researcher and former government adviser, said the recommendations by Trump and Health and Human Services Sec. Robert F. Kennedy Jr."are just not science based," and it’s irresponsible to cast doubt on a vaccine that protects against measles when the nation is facing its biggest epidemic in more than 30 years, according to the AP. Right now, there are no individual vaccines in the U.S. for measles, mumps or rubella. Every vaccine approved for those viruses by the Food and Drug Administration is combination shots. Local perspective: The Wisconsin DHS Secretary put out a statement on Thursday regarding the president's executive order, continuing to back previous guidance from public health officials that supports the current recommended MMR vaccine. "There is no new scientific evidence that justifies changing recommendations that have, and continue to, protect children across the United States," wrote DHS Secretary Kirsten Johnson. In February, Wisconsin was among states that sued the Trump administration over previous changes to federal childhood vaccine recommendations. The Source: Information from this article was sourced from the Wisconsin Department of Health Services, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, KFF, and the Associated Press. This story was reported from Eden Prairie, Minnesota. HealthWisconsinNews

news.content: Skip to content Skip to Audio Player Toggle Site Mobile Navigation Home News Shows Culture Music ABOUT Who We Are Events Careers / Volunteer LISTEN Stations & Schedules Music Playlists Ways to Listen SUPPORT Ways to Give Membership FAQ Funding Information CONTACT Get in Touch Help / FAQ Newsletters POLICIES Ethical Guidelines Policies and Reports Privacy Policy Public Inspection Files Public File Assistance News Shows Culture Music Wisconsin Public Radio Homepage Donate Search wpr.org Children’s Health, Health, News Measles outbreak grows to 36 confirmed, 3 probable cases in southwest Wisconsin Wisconsin DHS says 'no public exposure locations have been identified' By Evan Casey August 18, 2026 Updated August 18, 2026 at 5:27 pm A vial of the combination measles, mumps and rubella vaccine is prepared for a 12-month-old child at Tiger Pediatrics in Easley, S.C., on March 17, 2026. Mary Conlon/AP Photo The measles outbreak in southwestern Wisconsin has grown to 36 confirmed and three probable cases. Last week, the Wisconsin Department of Health Services said they were investigating 15 confirmed and six probable measles cases in Iowa County and Lafayette County. A Tuesday statement from the department said there are now two confirmed measles cases in Grant County as well. “Public health officials across each county continue the work to identify and notify people who may have been exposed to the measles virus,” the statement said. “At this time, no public exposure locations have been identified in connection with these cases.” Understanding Wisconsin, Together. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. Company This field is for validation purposes and should be left unchanged. Email Dr. Ryan Westergaard, chief medical officer with the Wisconsin DHS Bureau of Communicable Diseases, said a DHS team has been meeting multiple times a day to assist the county public health departments. He said local health officials are in charge of the investigation into the outbreak and have been doing interviews and facilitating testing. “And also giving vaccines out to people who are potentially exposed and at risk and don’t know their immunization status,” Westergaard said. The outbreak has been growing quickly. State officials first reported two confirmed cases in Lafayette and Iowa counties on Aug. 11. In the initial notification, state officials said the two people confirmed to have the virus appeared to have contracted it in Wisconsin “suggesting there may be additional measles cases in communities that have not yet been identified.” Two days later, the number of confirmed cases had grown to 15. According to state data, all but one of the people infected in the state this year have been unvaccinated. The majority are children 17 and under. Two people have been hospitalized. Measles is highly contagious and can be spread through the air. The state DHS statement said it, “can stay in the air for two hours after a sick person coughs or sneezes.” “Measles can cause serious health complications, including pneumonia, brain damage, and deafness, and can sometimes be deadly,” the statement said. The outbreak comes as new data from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention showed Wisconsin had low measles vaccination rates for kindergarten students. An estimated 85.1 percent of kindergarten students in Wisconsin had MMR vaccine coverage during the 2025-2026 school year, according to the CDC data. “We would like that to be higher,” Westergaard said. “The measles virus is one of the most contagious viruses that we have,” he added. “So it takes really high levels of vaccine coverage to prevent outbreaks when a case is present.” Westergaard said the rate of vaccination for the virus has gotten to a “dangerously low level in this country.” He said there’s only been small measles outbreaks in Wisconsin over the last two years. “But the current one is larger than we’ve had in the past several years,” he said. “So we’re working really hard to try to understand the extent, meaning how many people have been exposed and get the resources that they need, which is primarily vaccination to prevent the ongoing spread of measles in this community.” Two doses of the measles vaccine is 97 percent effective at preventing the virus, while one dose is 93 percent effective, according to the CDC. Westergaard encouraged people to check the Wisconsin Immunization Registry to see if they are up to date. “The best time to get vaccinated is before you’re exposed, but this is one of the vaccines that we can actually use after exposure too to prevent the likelihood of getting sick from measles,” Westergaard said. analysis.time: Event period: August 2026 (initial cases reported August 14; current update August 18, 2026). Publication date: August 18, 2026 at 5:27 pm.
analysis.location_and_population: Southwest Wisconsin, including Iowa County, Lafayette County, and Grant County. Affected population: predominantly children 17 years and under; all but one infected person unvaccinated. Two hospitalizations reported.
analysis.event: A measles outbreak confirmed by the Wisconsin Department of Health Services (DHS), with 36 confirmed and 3 probable cases as of August 18, 2026. The outbreak is under active investigation by local health officials with state DHS support.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: 36 confirmed cases, 3 probable cases, 2 hospitalizations. Measles is highly contagious via airborne transmission and can cause serious complications including pneumonia, brain damage, deafness, and death. Wisconsin kindergarten MMR vaccination coverage is 85.1% for 2025-2026, below herd immunity thresholds.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: DHS and county health departments are conducting interviews, facilitating testing, and providing post-exposure vaccination. No public exposure locations have been identified. State officials note the outbreak is larger than recent years and emphasize vaccination as the primary prevention tool. Investigation ongoing to determine exposure extent.

analysis.brief_en: A measles outbreak in southwest Wisconsin has expanded to 36 confirmed and three probable cases as of August 18, 2026, according to the Wisconsin Department of Health Services. The majority of cases involve unvaccinated children under 18, with two hospitalizations reported. State officials warn that Wisconsin’s kindergarten MMR vaccination rate of 85.1% falls short of the high coverage needed to prevent outbreaks, noting the current event is the largest in several years. Health authorities urge residents to verify immunization status via the Wisconsin Immunization Registry and receive vaccination if unprotected.

news.source_body_en: A measles outbreak in southwest Wisconsin has expanded to 36 confirmed and three probable cases as of August 18, 2026, according to the Wisconsin Department of Health Services. The majority of cases involve unvaccinated children under 18, with two hospitalizations reported. Public health teams are conducting contact tracing and offering post-exposure vaccinations, while no public exposure sites have been identified. State officials warn that Wisconsin’s kindergarten MMR vaccination rate of 85.1% falls short of the high coverage needed to prevent outbreaks, noting the current event is the largest in several years. Health authorities urge residents to verify immunization status via the Wisconsin Immunization Registry and receive vaccination if unprotected.

news.content: Skip to content 84° Parkersburg, WV News Weather Sports Livestream Obituaries WTAP+ Star-Spangled Sing-Off We the People Be Our Guest Home Be Our Guest Election Results Presidential Election Map West Virginia Interactive Results Ohio Interactive Results News Local Crime Politics / Elections Daybreak Regional National International Video Accidents Weather Radar Live Streaming Weather & Special Reports Closings Skycams WTAP Kid Cast Sports Futbol Frenzy Olympics Jan Dils Student Athlete of the Week Football Frenzy Scoreboard Obituaries WTAP+ Podcasts One Tank Trip In the Clouds with Jason Digital Exclusives We the People Contact Us Meet the Team Digital Advertising with WTAP Careers Purchase WTAP News Stories Download Our Mobile Apps Submit a Story Community Calendar WTAP Job Board Features and Contests Star-Spangled Sing-Off Athlete of the Week WTAP Kid Cast WTAP Cares Food Drive for Kids WTAP Health Check Daybreak Trivia Winners This Is Home Jan Dils Golden Apple Award Band of the Week Buy MOV First Churches Football Frenzy Pet Corner News Poll Academic Achiever Sports Poll Local News Live TV Listings NextGen TV Circle Country InvestigateTV Watching Your Wallet PowerNation User Content Digital Marketing Gray AI Policy Flood Warning is in effect Health officials talk Measles after four confirmed cases in Meigs County Close Health officials talk Measles after four confirmed cases in Meigs County By Cassidy Fury Published: Aug. 18, 2026 at 8:35 PM UTC Share Add Us On GoogleAdd as a preferred source on Google PARKERSBURG, W.Va. (WTAP) - Public health officials are urging residents in the Mid-Ohio Valley to remain vigilant following the confirmation of four active measles cases in Meigs County, Ohio. The Meigs County Health Department (MCHD) is currently tracing contacts and notifying individuals who may have been exposed. Local health agencies are warning that while there are currently no suspected cases or contacts under monitoring in West Virginia’s Mid-Ohio Valley, the region’s proximity and busy summer travel season increase the potential for cross-border transmission. Amy Phelps, Public Information Officer for the Mid-Ohio Valley Health Department, emphasized that travel is the primary driver of regional risk. “With the summer and people traveling, there’s always a chance that they could travel to an area where someone has measles,” Phelps said. “And if they don’t have immunity to it, they could catch it.” A Highly Contagious Airborne Threat Measles is one of the most contagious viruses known, spreading rapidly through person-to-person respiratory droplets. Health officials warn that the virus is exceptionally resilient, capable of lingering in the air of an enclosed room for up to two hours after an infected individual has left. Symptoms typically develop 7 to 14 days after exposure, though they can take up to 21 days to appear. The initial symptoms closely mimic other viral infections, starting with a high fever, cough, runny nose, and watery or red eyes similar to conjunctivitis. “About a couple days after those, then a lot of times people can get the white spots in the roof of their mouth,” Phelps explained. “And then a couple days after that is when the rash can start. And it usually starts on the head and then spreads downward.” Medical guidelines require infected individuals to remain isolated until at least five days after the initial appearance of the rash, at which point the virus is no longer transmissible. High Risks for Vulnerable Populations According to the Meigs County Health Department, approximately 20% of individuals who contract measles require hospitalization due to severe complications. These secondary infections occur because the virus severely weakens the body’s immune system. “Serious complications for measles is usually like younger children, generally five and under,” Phelps said. “And then older adults, people with compromised immune systems... they’re more apt to have secondary infections like pneumonia.” Other potential complications include severe dehydration and swelling of the brain (encephalitis). In pregnant women who have not received the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine, contracting the virus can lead to premature birth or low birth weight. Testing and Prevention Protocols Public health departments do not offer direct testing or treatment for measles. If residents suspect they have been exposed and begin experiencing symptoms, health officials warn against walking directly into clinics or emergency departments. “You don’t want people just showing up at the door generally,” Phelps said, noting that local healthcare clinics and hospitals have strict isolation protocols to prevent spreading the airborne pathogen. Patients are instructed to contact their primary care physician or hospital before arriving so proper precautions can be taken. For those unsure of their vaccination status, healthcare providers can perform a blood titer test to check for active antibodies. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends the MMR vaccine be administered in two doses: the first between 12 and 15 months of age, and the second between ages 4 and 6. Officials also noted a distinct demographic advantage for older residents: individuals born before 1957 are widely considered to have lifetime natural immunity to measles due to widespread exposure prior to the development of the vaccine. For families traveling with unvaccinated children or immunocompromised members, health department officials strongly advise monitoring outbreak databases and avoiding areas with documented active cases. (WTAP) - Public health officials are urging residents in the Mid-Ohio Valley to remain vigilant following the confirmation of four active measles cases in Meigs County, Ohio. The Meigs County Health Department (MCHD) is currently tracing contacts and notifying individuals who may have been exposed. Local health agencies are warning that while there are currently no suspected cases or contacts under monitoring in West Virginia’s Mid-Ohio Valley, the region’s proximity and busy summer travel season increase the potential for cross-border transmission. Amy Phelps, Public Information Officer for the Mid-Ohio Valley Health Department, emphasized that travel is the primary driver of regional risk. “With the summer and people traveling, there’s always a chance that they could travel to an area where someone has measles,” Phelps said. “And if they don’t have immunity to it, they could catch it.” A Highly Contagious Airborne Threat Measles is one of the most contagious viruses known, spreading rapidly through person-to-person respiratory droplets. Health officials warn that the virus is exceptionally resilient, capable of lingering in the air of an enclosed room for up to two hours after an infected individual has left. Symptoms typically develop 7 to 14 days after exposure, though they can take up to 21 days to appear. The initial symptoms closely mimic other viral infections, starting with a high fever, cough, runny nose, and watery or red eyes similar to conjunctivitis. “About a couple days after those, then a lot of times people can get the white spots in the roof of their mouth,” Phelps explained. “And then a couple days after that is when the rash can start. And it usually starts on the head and then spreads downward.” Medical guidelines require infected individuals to remain isolated until at least five days after the initial appearance of the rash, at which point the virus is no longer transmissible. High Risks for Vulnerable Populations According to the Meigs County Health Department, approximately 20% of individuals who contract measles require hospitalization due to severe complications. These secondary infections occur because the virus severely weakens the body’s immune system. “Serious complications for measles is usually like younger children, generally five and under,” Phelps said. “And then older adults, people with compromised immune systems... they’re more apt to have secondary infections like pneumonia.” Other potential complications include severe dehydration and swelling of the brain (encephalitis). In pregnant women who have not received the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine, contracting the virus can lead to premature birth or low birth weight. Testing and Prevention Protocols Public health departments do not offer direct testing or treatment for measles. If residents suspect they have been exposed and begin experiencing symptoms, health officials warn against walking directly into clinics or emergency departments. “You don’t want people just showing up at the door generally,” Phelps said, noting that local healthcare clinics and hospitals have strict isolation protocols to prevent spreading the airborne pathogen. Patients are instructed to contact their primary care physician or hospital before arriving so proper precautions can be taken. For those unsure of their vaccination status, healthcare providers can perform a blood titer test to check for active antibodies. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends the MMR vaccine be administered in two doses: the first between 12 and 15 months of age, and the second between ages 4 and 6. Officials also noted a distinct demographic advantage for older residents: individuals born before 1957 are widely considered to have lifetime natural immunity to measles due to widespread exposure prior to the development of the vaccine. For families traveling with unvaccinated children or immunocompromised members, health department officials strongly advise monitoring outbreak databases and avoiding areas with documented active cases. news.content_title: US measles cases surpass 2,000 for the 2nd year in a row: CDC
news.content: So far this year, 2,030 cases have been recorded in 38 states and D.C. ABC News medical correspondent Dr. Darien Sutton discusses the latest in the state's outbreak, which started last October. Measles outbreak in South Carolina is over, health officials say ABC News medical correspondent Dr. Darien Sutton discusses the latest in the state's outbreak, which started last October. Measles outbreak in South Carolina is over, health officials say ABC News medical correspondent Dr. Darien Sutton discusses the latest in the state's outbreak, which started last October. Measles outbreak in South Carolina is over, health officials say ABC News medical correspondent Dr. Darien Sutton discusses the latest in the state's outbreak, which started last October. Measles cases in the United States have surpassed 2,000 for the second year in a row, according to data updated Friday from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). So far in 2026, 2,030 confirmed cases have been recorded in 38 states and the District of Columbia, CDC data shows. Cases have been confirmed in: Alaska, Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Illinois, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Texas, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, Wisconsin and Wyoming. Just 10 measles cases were reported among international travelers so far this year, according to CDC data. Last year, 2,288 confirmed measles cases were reported for all of 2025. Prior to this, measles cases had not surpassed 2,000 in the U.S. since 1992. The U.S. also saw its first measles deaths in more than a decade last year, including two among unvaccinated school-aged children in Texas and one among an unvaccinated adult in New Mexico. The measles virus. BSIP/Universal Images Group via Getty Images The majority of measles cases in 2026 have been confirmed among children and teenagers aged 19 and younger, according to the CDC. About 92% of cases are among people who are unvaccinated or whose vaccination status is unknown, CDC data shows. Meanwhile, 4% of cases are among those who have received just one dose of the measles, mumps, rubella (MMR) vaccine and 4% of cases are among those who received the recommended two doses, according to the CDC. Dr. William Schaffner, a professor of preventive medicine at Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville, referred to the latest figures as "very disappointing and very concerning." "It indicates that an increasing number of parents are either postponing or withholding their children from vaccination, and this is very concerning because it permits this virus back now into in the United States to continue to spread and obviously to cause illness in the children affected," he told ABC News. January 2026 marked one year since measles cases were first detected on Texas. It’s unclear if the cases confirmed on Jan. 20, 2025, are linked to those that have been found other states; if so, it would mean the U.S. has seen a year of continuous transmission. If it's determined that the U.S. has experienced 12 months of continuous measles transmission, it could lead to a loss of the country's elimination status that was earned in 2000. Measles would once again be considered endemic or constantly circulating. The review of the measles elimination status in the U.S., which is determined by the Pan-American Health Organization, will take place in November 2026. Schaffner said the U.S.'s measles elimination status is threatened as a result of so many cases. "Measles, because it's the most contagious virus, is like the canary in the coal mine; it's the alert that lets us know that we're also opening ourselves up to other transmissible diseases that vaccines could prevent," he said. The CDC currently recommends that people receive two doses of the MMR vaccine, the first at ages 12 to 15 months and the second between 4 and 6 years old. One dose is 93% effective, and two doses are 97% effective against measles, the CDC says. However, CDC data show vaccination rates have been lagging in recent years. During the 2024 to 2025 school year, 92.5% of kindergartners received the MMR vaccine, according to data. This is lower than the 92.7% seen the previous school year and the 95.2% seen in the 2019 to 2020 school year, prior to the COVID-19 pandemic. Schaffner said that public health specialists need to listen carefully to parents who are skeptical or hesitant of getting their children vaccinated. "Have them speak to their own family doctors and pediatricians, have those conversations, and our pediatricians and family doctors have to provide a level of comfort and reassurance," he said. "Facts are fundamental, but more importantly, these parents need reassurance and a level of comfort that what their doctors ... are recommending is in the best interest of their child and the communities in which their children live." "These diseases are bad and can be really bad. The vaccines are good and really good," Schaffner added

news.content_original: So far this year, 2,030 cases have been recorded in 38 states and D.C. Measles outbreak in South Carolina is over, health officials say ABC News medical correspondent Dr. Darien Sutton discusses the latest in the state's outbreak, which started last October. Measles cases in the United States have surpassed 2,000 for the second year in a row, according to data updated Friday from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). So far in 2026, 2,030 confirmed cases have been recorded in 38 states and the District of Columbia, CDC data shows. Cases have been confirmed in: Alaska, Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Illinois, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Texas, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, Wisconsin and Wyoming. Just 10 measles cases were reported among international travelers so far this year, according to CDC data. Last year, 2,288 confirmed measles cases were reported for all of 2025. Prior to this, measles cases had not surpassed 2,000 in the U.S. since 1992. The U.S. also saw its first measles deaths in more than a decade last year, including two among unvaccinated school-aged children in Texas and one among an unvaccinated adult in New Mexico. The measles virus. BSIP/Universal Images Group via Getty Images The majority of measles cases in 2026 have been confirmed among children and teenagers aged 19 and younger, according to the CDC. About 92% of cases are among people who are unvaccinated or whose vaccination status is unknown, CDC data shows. Meanwhile, 4% of cases are among those who have received just one dose of the measles, mumps, rubella (MMR) vaccine and 4% of cases are among those who received the recommended two doses, according to the CDC. Dr. William Schaffner, a professor of preventive medicine at Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville, referred to the latest figures as "very disappointing and very concerning." "It indicates that an increasing number of parents are either postponing or withholding their children from vaccination, and this is very concerning because it permits this virus back now into in the United States to continue to spread and obviously to cause illness in the children affected," he told ABC News. January 2026 marked one year since measles cases were first detected on Texas. It’s unclear if the cases confirmed on Jan. 20, 2025, are linked to those that have been found other states; if so, it would mean the U.S. has seen a year of continuous transmission. If it's determined that the U.S. has experienced 12 months of continuous measles transmission, it could lead to a loss of the country's elimination status that was earned in 2000. Measles would once again be considered endemic or constantly circulating. The review of the measles elimination status in the U.S., which is determined by the Pan-American Health Organization, will take place in November 2026. Schaffner said the U.S.'s measles elimination status is threatened as a result of so many cases. "Measles, because it's the most contagious virus, is like the canary in the coal mine; it's the alert that lets us know that we're also opening ourselves up to other transmissible diseases that vaccines could prevent," he said. The CDC currently recommends that people receive two doses of the MMR vaccine, the first at ages 12 to 15 months and the second between 4 and 6 years old. One dose is 93% effective, and two doses are 97% effective against measles, the CDC says. However, CDC data show vaccination rates have been lagging in recent years. During the 2024 to 2025 school year, 92.5% of kindergartners received the MMR vaccine, according to data. This is lower than the 92.7% seen the previous school year and the 95.2% seen in the 2019 to 2020 school year, prior to the COVID-19 pandemic. Schaffner said that public health specialists need to listen carefully to parents who are skeptical or hesitant of getting their children vaccinated. "Have them speak to their own family doctors and pediatricians, have those conversations, and our pediatricians and family doctors have to provide a level of comfort and reassurance," he said. "Facts are fundamental, but more importantly, these parents need reassurance and a level of comfort that what their doctors ... are recommending is in the best interest of their child and the communities in which their children live." "These diseases are bad and can be really bad. The vaccines are good and really good," Schaffner added

analysis.brief_en: U.S. measles cases have exceeded 2,000 for the second straight year, with 2,030 confirmed cases reported across 38 states and Washington, D.C. as of August 2026, according to CDC data. The outbreak, which began in January 2026, has disproportionately affected unvaccinated children and teenagers, with 92% of cases occurring in individuals who are unvaccinated or whose vaccination status is unknown. Last year’s total of 2,288 cases included the nation’s first measles deaths in over a decade. Health officials warn that sustained transmission could jeopardize the U.S. measles elimination status, with a critical review by the Pan-American Health Organization slated for November 2026. Vaccination coverage among kindergartners has declined to 92.5%, below pre-pandemic levels, prompting calls for strengthened public health messaging and provider engagement to counter vaccine hesitancy.

Newsletters♡Donate Now Menu Search Sign in Menu Programs & Podcasts Schedule Ways to Give Search Sign in Minnesota Now with Nina Moini Kelly Gordon and Ngoc Bui August 20, 2026 2:52 PM Minnesota kindergartners have third lowest measles vaccination rate in U.S. Vaccination rates among kindergartners in Minnesota have steadily declined since 2020. Patrick T. Fallon | AFP via Getty Images file ListenMinnesota kindergartners have third lowest measles vaccination rate in U.S. Go Deeper. Create an account or log in to save stories. Log in Like this? Thanks for liking this story! We have added it to a list of your favorite stories. Show me! Save Share As kids start looking ahead to the new school year, health officials are looking at new immunization data — and it’s showing rates have continued to fall over the last year especially in Minnesota. Kindergartners in our state have the second and third lowest vaccination levels in the country for DTaP and MMR, respectively, at 86 percent for both. These two vaccines are combination shots that protect against a myriad of diseases like whooping cough and measles. Minnesota also has one of the highest exemption rates at 6.9 percent. Dr. Andrea Singh, chair of pediatrics at HealthPartners and Park Nicollet, said these numbers reflect what she’s been seeing in her office. Turn Up Your Support MPR News helps you turn down the noise and build shared understanding. Turn up your support for this public resource and keep trusted journalism accessible to all. “More and more in a clinic setting, we’re getting a lot of parents that are questioning the need for vaccinations or the motivation behind vaccines.” She said there are numerous factors that could be leading to the decline but noted in Minnesota particularly there was a campaign in the late 1990s and 2000s. “There was a very targeted effort by some anti-vaccination groups to talk to immigrant communities and make some unfounded links between MMR vaccines, in particular, and the likelihood that your child would have autism.” The major concern from health officials as rates fall for the MMR vaccination is the loss of what’s called “herd immunity.” That’s when at least 90 percent of the population is vaccinated in order to protect those who haven’t been vaccinated or more vulnerable populations. Dr. Singh said what many might not know is that measles is one of the most contagious and dangerous diseases. One person with measles could spread it to 10 to 12 people if they’re breathing the same air. It can also lead to other serious illness like subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, a degenerative and almost always deadly brain disease that appears years after recovery from measles. Earlier this month, President Donald Trump signed an executive order calling for the revamping of the childhood vaccine schedule. As the public sentiment and policies around vaccinations continue to shift, Dr. Singh said it’s important for people — especially those who may have concerns about vaccines — to talk with a trusted medical provider. “Ask the questions, don’t be scared,” Dr. Singh. “Ask and we can help work with you on helping to make you comfortable. But we know 100 percent that vaccines, in general, are safe and they save lives.” Use the audio player above to listen to the full conversation. news.content: Friday, August 2180°F / Ithaca Sign IneNewsletter News Sports Business Education Lifestyle Opinion Spotlight Events Submit Your Event Public Notices Sign In eNewsletter Directory E-Editions Obituaries Advertise Event Submission Hometown Heroes Hometown Heroes Submission Made in Tompkins News Sports Opinion Business Education Lifestyle Spotlight Events Newsletter News August 18, 2026 Measles cases on rise in neighboring counties Measles cases are rising in Tioga and Seneca counties, prompting Tompkins County Whole Health to urge residents to ensure they are fully vaccinated. Tompkins County Whole Health (TCWH) is alerting the community that measles cases are on the rise in neighboring counties, including Tioga and Seneca Counties. Measles is a highly contagious virus and spreads rapidly among those who are unvaccinated. Being unvaccinated increases risks for severe complications, hospitalization and death. Those most at risk of infection include unvaccinated infants, children or adults (excluding those who were born before 1957, who are considered immune), pregnant persons, and those with weakened immune systems. TCWH urges everyone to be vaccinated against measles. A complete vaccination (two-dose series of MMR (Measles, Mumps, Rubella) vaccine) is safe and effective at preventing infection. The measles virus is easily spread through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes or by direct contact with a contaminated surface. Symptoms can take from 7 days up to 21 days from exposure to occur. Measles can often be mistaken for other respiratory illnesses, as symptoms include a high fever, cough, runny or congested nose, sore throat and watery eyes. A red and blotchy rash may occur within 3-5 days following the start of cold-like symptoms, with the rash usually appearing on the face first. The rash may spread down the neck, trunk, arms, legs and feet, and spots may join together as they spread. When the rash appears, fever temperatures may rise above 104° Fahrenheit. If you suspect you were exposed to measles, contact our Division of Community Health at 607-274-6604. Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for measles may be given within 72 hours of exposure to prevent infection or lessen the severity of the disease in people who do not have immunity and were exposed to the virus. If you develop symptoms, please call your healthcare provider or contact our office. Let the provider or answering service know that you have been exposed to measles or what symptoms you are experiencing. Please do not go to the Emergency Room, Urgent Care, or a doctor’s office without first calling to avoid potentially exposing other people to measles. Because measles can spread quickly and easily through the air, it is very important to seek advice over the phone first to reduce risk of further spreading the virus. This also gives healthcare facilities an opportunity to take safety measures, such as placing you in an isolated room immediately, to prevent spreading the virus to other vulnerable patients in the waiting room or other areas. Do not fill this field Sign Up Verified Complications from measles are serious and include very high fever, ear infections, pneumonia, and encephalitis (swelling of the brain). Risks also include permanent loss of hearing, vision, and the development of learning disabilities. There is no cure for measles, only treatment for symptom relief. Measles is especially dangerous for those who are unvaccinated, for young children, and for those who are immunocompromised. TCWH Medical Director Dr. William Klepack stated, “Measles is a terrible virus with a very high infection rate in unvaccinated populations. The MMR vaccine is 97% effective at preventing infection. This means that while the vaccine is very effective at preventing illness, there is a risk that 3 out of every 100 vaccinated people could still become infected. The risk if you are not vaccinated is much greater.” Dr. Klepack continued, “We strongly encourage families to make sure their children, especially those under age 5, stay up to date on their vaccination schedule. Children should get their first MMR shot at 12 through 15 months old (as soon as possible within this time-period). The second dose may be given as soon as one month after the first dose but is typically given between 4 and 6 years of age. At this time, there is no need to seek early vaccination for your infant and maintaining the routine immunization schedule is advised.” TCWH advises all who have not been vaccinated against measles or have had only one dose to contact their healthcare provider or our office to get up to date with their vaccinations. Call our office at 607-274-6604 or visit our website to learn more about Whole Health’s Community Health Division and Immunization Clinics: https://www.tompkinscountyny.gov/health/immunizations Learn more about measles by visiting Whole Health’s measles webpage: tompkinscountyny.gov/All-Departments/Whole-Health/Community-Health-Services/Communicable-Disease/Measles Story Tags Wellness Community News Local News Tompkins County Related News 17h ago County Board of Elections moving to 214 W. analysis.time: Published on August 18, 2026; event reported as ongoing with no specific event date provided in the evidence.
analysis.location_and_population: Tioga County and Seneca County, New York, USA; alert issued by Tompkins County Whole Health (TCWH) for residents in the region.
analysis.event: Measles cases are reported as rising in neighboring counties (Tioga and Seneca), prompting an official public health alert from TCWH urging vaccination. The event is confirmed as a reported increase in cases, not an outbreak in Tompkins County itself.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Not reported in the supplied evidence regarding case counts, deaths, or exposures in Tioga or Seneca counties. Risk is explicitly stated as high for unvaccinated individuals, including severe complications such as pneumonia, encephalitis, permanent hearing or vision loss, and learning disabilities. Measles is described as highly contagious with a 97% vaccine effectiveness rate, leaving a 3% risk of infection even in vaccinated individuals.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: TCWH is urging all residents to ensure they are fully vaccinated with the MMR vaccine (two-dose series). Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is recommended within 72 hours of exposure for unvaccinated individuals. Guidance includes contacting health authorities for suspected exposure, avoiding healthcare facilities without prior notification to prevent spread, and maintaining routine immunization schedules for infants and children. No specific investigation status or case counts are provided in the evidence.

analysis.brief_en: Public health officials in upstate New York are warning of a rise in measles cases in neighboring Tioga and Seneca counties, prompting Tompkins County Whole Health to urge residents to verify their vaccination status. Measles, a highly contagious respiratory virus, poses severe risks—including pneumonia, brain swelling, and permanent disabilities—for unvaccinated individuals, particularly infants, young children, pregnant persons, and those with weakened immune systems. The MMR vaccine remains 97% effective, though a small risk of infection persists even in vaccinated people. Authorities advise contacting healthcare providers immediately if exposed and avoiding emergency rooms or clinics without prior notice to prevent further transmission. Routine childhood immunization schedules are emphasized, with the first MMR dose recommended at 12–15 months and the second between ages 4 and 6.

news.source_body_en: Public health officials in upstate New York are warning of a rise in measles cases in neighboring Tioga and Seneca counties, prompting Tompkins County Whole Health to urge residents to verify their vaccination status. Measles, a highly contagious respiratory virus, poses severe risks—including pneumonia, brain swelling, and permanent disabilities—for unvaccinated individuals, particularly infants, young children, pregnant persons, and those with weakened immune systems. The MMR vaccine remains 97% effective, though a small risk of infection persists even in vaccinated people. Authorities advise contacting healthcare providers immediately if exposed and avoiding emergency rooms or clinics without prior notice to prevent further transmission. Routine childhood immunization schedules are emphasized, with the first MMR dose recommended at 12–15 months and the second between ages 4 and 6.
